record.body: Sound level is measured in decibels, a logarithmic scale referenced to a standard pressure, and the signal-to-noise ratio, or SNR, measures how far a target sound stands above background noise. A call at 60 decibels against background noise at 50 decibels has an SNR of 10 decibels, which is usually easy to detect, while the same call against 58 decibels of noise has an SNR of only 2 decibels and may be missed. Because decibels are logarithmic, adding two equal sounds raises the level by only about 3 decibels, not by doubling the decibel number, and a 10-decibel rise is perceived as roughly a doubling of loudness. Noise measurement matters for all three layers: biophony is the signal, while geophony and anthrophony are usually the noise, though in soundscape ecology all three are studied in their own right.

demo.code:
TITLE = 'Measuring Noise: Levels and Signal-to-Noise Ratio'
import math
A = 60
B = 60
tot = 10 * math.log10(10 ** (A / 10.0) + 10 ** (B / 10.0))
print('Record: ' + TITLE)
print('Level one: %.1f decibels' % A)
print('Level two: %.1f decibels' % B)
print('Combined level: %.1f decibels' % tot)
print('Note: decibels add logarithmically, never by plain addition.')
demo.expected_output:
Record: Measuring Noise: Levels and Signal-to-Noise Ratio
Level one: 60.0 decibels
Level two: 60.0 decibels
Combined level: 63.0 decibels
Note: decibels add logarithmically, never by plain addition.
